q: Trace what happened to Australian wine in the Chinese market between 2020 and 2024, and what it did to the industry at home.
accept: anti-dumping duties in 2021 removed in 2024 after exports collapsed
chinese tariffs of up to 218 percent lifted in march 2024
duties destroyed the largest export market then were removed in 2024
five year duties from 2021 lifted early leaving a red wine glut
ans: China opened anti-dumping and countervailing investigations in 2020, imposed provisional duties that November and confirmed final duties of roughly 116 to 218 per cent in March 2021, set to run five years. China had become Australia's largest export market by value, and it closed almost overnight: shipments fell from over a billion dollars a year to near nothing. The consequences landed hardest on red grapes and on the warm inland regions that had scaled up to supply that trade — prices collapsed, unsold red wine piled up, and growers began pulling vines again. The duties were lifted at the end of March 2024, but distribution channels had been taken by Chile, France and others, and the recovery has been partial rather than a return.
exp: The commercial lesson is concentration risk: one market took a third of export value and the industry had built vineyards against it. Note also the asymmetry of recovery — a tariff can be removed by decree, a shelf position cannot.

q: Explain why the Coonawarra boundary ended up in court, and what that tells you about Australia's GI system.
accept: a decade of appeals over whether the line should follow terra rossa soil
litigated through the aat and federal court over where the gi line ran
the fight was soil purity versus established growers on the fringes
boundary is all the law contains so the boundary was worth suing over
ans: Coonawarra's GI was determined in the late 1990s and immediately appealed, and the fight ran through the Administrative Appeals Tribunal and the Federal Court into the early 2000s. The dispute was whether the boundary should trace the terra rossa over limestone — a geological line that would have excluded long-established growers on black soil and sand — or follow the practical reality of who had been farming and selling as Coonawarra for decades. Land values and brand value both hung on it. The final line is broader than the pure terra rossa cigar. The systemic point is that because an Australian GI regulates the boundary and nothing else — no variety, no yield, no method — the boundary carries the entire value of the name, so it is the only thing worth litigating.
exp: Compare France, where an AOC withholds so much else — grape, density, ripeness, ageing — that the map is only part of the value. Where the map is the whole law, expect lawyers.

q: Tell the story of Grange's creation, and explain what makes it philosophically un-French.
accept: max schubert from 1951 with hidden vintages and multi-region shiraz in american oak
schubert 1951 secretly continued 1957 to 1959 and reinstated with the 1960
a blend across regions in new american oak so a style not a place
penfolds house style blended across south australia rather than a single vineyard
ans: Max Schubert, Penfolds' chief winemaker, toured Europe in 1950 studying Bordeaux and came home wanting a wine that would still be alive in fifty years. Lacking Cabernet in quantity and lacking French oak, he used Shiraz and new American oak hogsheads, and made the first experimental vintage in 1951. The board and the Sydney tasting establishment condemned the wines at showings in 1957 and ordered him to stop; he made the 1957, 1958 and 1959 in secret, and when the earlier vintages came round in bottle the decision was reversed, the wine officially reinstated with the 1960. It is blended across South Australian districts, usually with a small proportion of Cabernet, and finished in new American oak. So it is a house style and a bin number, not a site: it argues that blending across regions to a consistent ideal is a legitimate route to greatness, which is the exact opposite of the cru principle.
exp: Every question about Australian classification eventually meets this wine: the country's greatest red cannot carry a single regional GI, and nobody thinks less of it for that. Have the contrast ready in one sentence.

q: How is Tasmania structured as a GI, and what are its working districts?
accept: one gi for the whole island with informal districts like tamar and coal river
a single region with no registered subregions tamar pipers coal river derwent
tasmania is one gi and every district name is unofficial
legally one region though the trade uses tamar valley pipers river and the rest
ans: Tasmania is a single GI covering the whole island — one zone, one region, and no registered subregions whatsoever, so every district name you see is informal. In practice the trade divides it into the Tamar Valley and Pipers River in the north, the East Coast, and the Coal River Valley, Derwent Valley and Huon or Channel in the south, with a small North West. The north is warmer and drier and ripens Pinot Noir more fully; the Coal River Valley is the driest part of the state and depends on irrigation; the Huon is the coolest and a natural sparkling-base source. The state produces a tiny share of Australia's crush but a disproportionate share of its sparkling base and its finest cool-climate Pinot and Chardonnay.
exp: A candidate who recites Tamar Valley and Coal River as though they were GIs has made a legal error in front of a Master. Say the districts, then say they are not registered — the qualification is the point being tested.

q: The Hunter Valley should not work on paper. Explain why it does.
accept: subtropical and wet but saved by cloud cover sea breezes and early picking
humid climate offset by afternoon cloud and picking semillon very early
effective heat is far lower than the averages suggest so the wines stay medium bodied
cloud and maritime influence plus deliberate early harvest for low alcohol semillon
ans: It is humid subtropical at about 32.5 degrees south, hot, with much of its rain arriving in summer and at harvest, and serious disease pressure — on the numbers it looks like a region that should not make fine wine. Three things rescue it. Afternoon cloud cover cuts effective sunshine hours and heat during ripening, so the mean temperature overstates the stress on the vine. Sea breezes reach it from the Pacific. And growers pick early, deliberately. Semillon comes in around 10.5 to 11 per cent potential alcohol, ahead of the rain and ahead of flavour ripeness, is made without oak and without malolactic, and then transforms over fifteen to twenty years into toast, honey and lanolin. Shiraz on the sandy alluvial flats and red volcanic soils stays medium-bodied, savoury and earthy, closer to the Rhône than to the Barossa.
exp: The takeaway is that climate indices built on mean temperature mislead badly in cloudy, humid places. The Hunter is the standing counter-example, and the reason Hunter Semillon has no true analogue anywhere else.

q: Where did sparkling Shiraz come from, and how is it made and served?
accept: great western in victoria where charles pierlot brought the champagne method in 1890
victorian sparkling burgundy made from shiraz finished with red wine dosage
hans irvine hired pierlot at great western and seppelt later took it over
seppelt at great western traditional method red sparkling from the 1890s
a traditional method red needing dosage to balance tannin served chilled
ans: From Great Western in Victoria. Hans Irvine, who bought Joseph Best's cellars in 1888, brought the Champenois Charles Pierlot out in 1890, and without Pinot Noir in any quantity he applied the traditional method to the red grapes at hand; Seppelt acquired the business in 1918 and made the style its own. The wine sold for a century under the name sparkling Burgundy, which EU traditional-term protection eventually forced Australia to abandon. The serious versions are traditional method: Shiraz picked for flavour rather than for acid, given long time on lees, and finished with a generous dosage — often using aged red wine — because the sugar is what balances the tannin and the tannin is what makes the style unlike any other sparkling wine. Seppelt's Show Sparkling and Rockford's Black Shiraz are the reference points. Serve it lightly chilled, and the Australian ritual is with Christmas turkey in midsummer heat.
exp: Two exam threads meet here: an Australian style with a genuine 19th-century pedigree, and a name lost to EU traditional terms — the same law that turned Australian 'port' into tawny and 'sherry' into apera. Irvine, not Seppelt, hired Pierlot; Seppelt bought Great Western in 1918, which is why the wine carries its name today.

q: Explain the 1985 scandal, the substance, and the reform it forced.
accept: diethylene glycol 1985 antifreeze strictest wine law

ans: Diethylene glycol added to fake body in sweet wines; exports collapsed, and Austria wrote one of the world's strictest wine laws in response
exp: The industry rebuilt around dry, terroir-driven quality — the scandal made modern Austria.
